---
order: 2
unit: drawing
introduces: [repeat]
title: Repeat with a loop
summary: Predict, run and change short programs that repeat lines with a loop.
language: python
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground" 8123
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8123/index.html
  ready: Python code
  layout: full
pacing:
  keyDelayMs: 30
hook: "Loops are how a program draws 100 tiles, sends 100 emails or reads 100 sensors without 100 lines of code."
voice: true
explainClip:
  query: { code: "", speed: 6 }
  caption: "A loop repeats lines, so you write them once"
  say: "A program runs from the top down, and a loop repeats lines for you."
  pacing: { keyDelayMs: 22 }
  clip:
    - type: { into: "Python code", text: "from turtle import *\n\n", append: true }
    - caption:
        text: "for i in range(4): does the indented lines 4 times."
        say: "A for loop does the lines indented under it, here four times."
    - type: { into: "Python code", text: "for i in range(4):\n", append: true }
    - caption:
        text: "forward(100) draws a line. right(90) turns a quarter turn."
        say: "forward 100 draws a line, and right 90 turns a quarter of a full turn."
    - type: { into: "Python code", text: "    forward(100)\n    right(90)\n", append: true }
    - click: "Run"
    - expect: { selector: "#status", contains: "Finished" }
    - caption:
        text: "4 turns of 90 make one full turn: 360 degrees."
        say: "Four turns of 90 degrees add up to one full turn, 360 degrees."
    - wait: 1200
    - expect: { selector: "#turtle-state", contains: "heading 0" }
---
Last lesson you drew digits by writing every command one after another. A square written that way takes eight lines. There is a shorter way.

## Predict

```step
stage: predict
code: square.py#loop
reveal: true
check:
  type: predict
  q: "What will the turtle draw?"
  options: ["a square", "one long line", "one side, then a turn", "nothing, because i is never used"]
  fault: logic
  misconception: loop-body-indent
  actual: "A square. The two indented lines run 4 times: a side of 100, then a quarter turn, four times over. The turtle finishes where it started, facing right."
app: true
clip:
  - caption: The turtle starts in the middle, facing right.
  - type:
      into: Python code
      text: "@square.py#loop"
  - click: Run
  - expect: { selector: "#status", contains: Finished }
  - expect: { selector: "#turtle-state", contains: "heading 0" }
```

The line `for i in range(4):` is new. What do you think the turtle will draw?

## Run

```step
stage: run
code: square.py#loop
try: { starter: "square.py#loop", height: 420 }
```

Run the program and compare it with your prediction. Which lines ran four times?

Here is what each line does.

| Line | What it does | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `for i in range(4):` | Starts a loop that runs four times | `range(4)` counts 0, 1, 2, 3: one run each |
| `    forward(100)` | Draws a side | It is indented, so it is part of the loop |
| `    right(90)` | Turns a quarter turn | Also indented, so it repeats too |

Without the loop, the same square is eight lines. The loop writes the pattern once, and the count is a number you can change.

## Investigate

```step
stage: investigate
code: square.py#compare
insight: "Repetition has a cost: without a loop the code grows with every side, and a loop does the same work with a number you can change."
app: true
clip:
  - type:
      into: Python code
      text: "@square.py#loop"
  - click: Run
  - expect: { selector: "#status", contains: Finished }
tasks:
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "A square drawn one command at a time uses 8 lines of drawing code. A 20-sided shape drawn the same way would use how many lines?"
      answer: 40
      explain: "Each side needs 2 lines (forward and a turn), so 20 sides need 40."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: square.py#bug
      text: "This was meant to draw a square. Instead the turtle draws one long line and turns once at the very end. Click the wrong line."
      answer: 5
      fault: logic
      misconception: loop-body-indent
      explain: "right(90) is not indented, so it is not part of the loop. The loop draws four sides in a straight line, and the turn runs once afterwards. Indent it under the for line so both lines repeat."
  - check:
      type: trace
      slideCode: square.py#loop
      text: "for i in range(4): makes a counter called i. It starts at 0 and goes up by 1 each time round the loop. Fill in the table for the square."
      table: |
        | pass | i | turned so far |
        | 1 | 0 | 90 |
        | 2 | [1] | [180] |
        | 3 | [2] | [270] |
        | 4 | [3] | [360] |
      explain: "i counts 0, 1, 2, 3: four passes, starting from 0. This square never uses i, but it is there, and later programs will use it. After four turns of 90 the turtle has turned 360 degrees, a full turn."
```

Compare the two programs. They draw the same square.

### Count the lines

How much code does each way need as the shape gets more sides?

### Spot the bug

Indented lines belong to the loop. Find the line that should repeat but doesn't.

### Follow the counter

In `for i in range(4):`, the name `i` is a counter. Follow it round the loop.

## Modify

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Change a working program one small step at a time and check each result; the turn angle comes from the shape, not from guessing."
try: { starter: "square.py#modify", height: 420 }
app: true
query: { code: "@square.py#triangle", view: output, autorun: 1 }
clip:
  - wait: 600
  - expect: { selector: "#status", contains: Finished }
  - expect: { selector: "#turtle-state", contains: "heading 0" }
caption: "The expected result: a triangle"
reveal: Show what the triangle should look like
hint:
  - "A square turns the turtle 90 degrees four times. How many times does a triangle turn, and what do all the turns add up to?"
  - "Two numbers change: how many times the loop repeats, and how far the turtle turns each time."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I changed the loop so it draws a triangle." }
```

Change the loop so it draws a triangle instead of a square. Run after each change.

## Make

```step
stage: make
try: { starter: "square.py#make", height: 420 }
app: true
query: { code: "@square.py#sol-stairs", view: output, autorun: 1 }
clip:
  - wait: 600
  - expect: { selector: "#status", contains: Finished }
caption: "The expected result: a staircase with 5 steps"
reveal: Show what the staircase should look like
hint:
  - "Trace one step with your finger. Which moves and turns make one step?"
  - "One step is four lines: up, turn, across, turn back. Put those under a for line."
check: { type: code, text: "Draw a staircase with 5 steps using a loop.", rules: { loops: 1 } }
unlocks: [for-loop]
smaller:
  check:
    type: question
    q: "A staircase has 5 steps. Which part goes under the for line?"
    options:
      - "One step: up, turn, across, turn back"
      - "All five steps, one after another"
      - "Just the line going up"
      - "Only the turns"
    answer: 0
    feedback:
      - null
      - "The loop is what makes the five. Write one step, and say how many times."
      - "A step also needs the line across, or it never gets any further along."
      - "The lines matter as much as the turns: a step is both."
    explain: "Find the part that repeats, write it once, and let the loop do the counting."
```

A loop works for any pattern, not only shapes. Find the part that repeats, write it once, and say how many times.

Draw a staircase with 5 steps, like the picture. When it works, change one number to make it 10 steps. Then try a pattern of your own: a zigzag, a row of battlements or a dashed line. Find the part that repeats first.

Next lesson adds variables. Then you put loops and variables to work on a whole program: a street of houses.

```teacher
summary: Students see that the square they drew with eight lines can be written
  with three, using a loop, and find out how to change the count and the turn.
time: 35
timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 8 min · Make 7 min
goals:
  - I can use a loop to repeat lines instead of copying them.
  - I can say which lines belong to a loop.
  - I can work out the turn for a shape with any number of sides.
before: >
  Open the lesson, run the first program and draw the triangle from the Modify
  step yourself. It takes about five minutes and you will meet the same surprise
  students do: the turn is 120 degrees, not 60.
running:
  - "Predict: show the loop and ask what it draws. Take two or three answers
    before anyone runs it; each wrong option is a different idea of what a loop
    repeats (only the first line, only once, nothing because i is unused)."
  - "Run: run it live on the slide, then students run it on their own screens
    and compare with their prediction. Ask: which lines ran four times, and how
    do you know? Then show the eight-line square beside the loop."
  - "Investigate: the key idea is that a loop does the same work as copied
    lines, but stays the same size. Ask a student to say why the loop version is
    easier to change. The bug task (right(90) not indented) comes after students
    have seen the loop work. The trace task traces the counter i (0, 1, 2, 3);
    say that it counts from 0, because later lessons use it."
  - "Modify: work the triangle live on the slide first if the room is unsure,
    then let students go on alone. Let them get it wrong first. If they try 60
    degrees, ask them to walk the shape themselves: how far do you turn at each
    corner?"
  - "Make: the staircase reverses the lesson: students find the part that
    repeats in a picture and write it once. Early finishers can try the house (a
    square, then a roof turning left 60 and right 120)."
stuck:
  - see: The triangle has a gap, or the shape looks like a star.
    ask: How many times does the loop repeat, and how far does the turtle turn each
      time?
    fix: A shape with 3 sides repeats 3 times and turns 120 degrees. All the turns
      add up to 360.
  - see: Only the first line repeats, or the program stops with an indentation
      error.
    ask: Which lines are pushed in under the for line?
    fix: The lines that repeat must be indented (four spaces) under the for line.
  - see: A student types forward(100) and right(90) many times and sees no reason to
      change.
    ask: How long would that be for a 50-sided shape?
    fix: Ask them to draw a 50-sided shape both ways. The loop stays 3 lines; the
      copied version needs 100.
stretch: Draw a shape with 50 sides and turn 360 / 50 degrees. What does it
  start to look like, and why?
support: Give the loop version and ask the student to change only one number at
  a time, running after each change.
leads: "Loops come back in every lesson, and in tessellations, logo design and
  generative art. Next lesson stores numbers in variables, so the turn can be
  worked out instead of guessed. Then A street of houses reads a whole program
  that uses both. Class ideas: design a floor tile and repeat it; recreate a
  simple logo from code."
exit:
  q: A turtle draws a shape with 5 equal sides using a loop. How many times does
    the loop repeat, and how far does the turtle turn each time?
  a: 5 times, turning 72 degrees each time (360 divided by 5).
explain: >
  A **loop** repeats the lines indented under it. `for i in range(4):` means "do
  the indented lines 4 times". Instead of writing the same two lines four times,
  you write them once and say how often. The name `i` is a counter that takes
  the values 0, 1, 2, 3 on the four passes. A square does not use it, but later
  programs do.


  `forward(100)` moves the turtle 100 steps and draws a line. `right(90)` turns
  it on the spot, a quarter of a full turn.


  To close any shape, the turtle turns all the way round once in total: 360
  degrees. Split that between the corners: 360 ÷ 4 = 90 for a square, 360 ÷ 3 =
  120 for a triangle.
solutions:
  step-4: square.py#sol-triangle
  step-5: square.py#sol-stairs
struggle: Working out the turn angle for a shape. Ask how far the turtle turns
  in total and how many turns there are, instead of giving the number.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Would you rather give a robot 100 separate instructions, or one instruction
      to repeat 100 times? What could go wrong with each?
    prompts:
      - Which is easier to change if the plan changes?
      - Which is easier to get wrong without noticing?
      - Is there ever a time copying the lines would be the better choice?
    notes: "Let students defend both sides. Copying wins when each step is
      different, when you will only ever do it once, or when a reader needs to
      see every step. The loop wins when the steps are the same and the count
      may change. Return to this after the staircase Make: did anyone choose
      copying, and why?"
  activities:
    - at: start
      kind: info
      title: By the end of this lesson
      do: >
        Here is a shape drawn by 3 lines of Python. By the end of the lesson you
        will write programs like it.
      notes: "Run the 36-sided shape from the stretch task on the projector (for i in
        range(36): forward(20) right(10)) before anything else. Ask: how many
        lines of code do you think that took?"
    - at: investigate
      title: Play turtle
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        One volunteer is the turtle, standing in the middle facing the window.

        The class reads the loop aloud, one line at a time. The turtle obeys: 3
        steps for forward(100), a quarter turn for right(90).

        Now try it with range(3) and right(120). Where does the turtle end up?
      notes: "Papert designed the turtle so learners could play it. Walking the shape
        makes two things concrete: only the indented lines repeat, and a closed
        shape turns all the way round (360). If the turtle turns 60 for the
        triangle, ask the class to watch which way they end up facing."
    - at: modify
      title: "Optional: pairs at one computer"
      do: >
        One person types (driver), the other reads the task and checks each run
        (navigator).

        Swap at every new shape.
      notes: Pair programming keeps both students thinking and talking, and it helps
        students who are less confident.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Count the changes
      type: number
      slideCode: square.py#loop
      q: The loop version draws a 20-sided shape. How many numbers in it change?
      answer: 2
      explain: Only range(20) and the turn (360 / 20 = 18 degrees). The loop is the
        same 3 lines.
    - at: investigate
      title: Which way now?
      type: question
      slideCode: square.py#loop
      q: The turtle starts in the middle, facing right. After the square, which way is
        it facing?
      options:
        - Up
        - Down
        - Right
        - Left
      answer: 2
      explain: Four turns of 90 make 360 degrees, a full turn, so the turtle faces
        right again. Any shape that closes up turns 360 degrees in total.
  self-regulation:
    card: code-read-the-error
    mode: teach
    at: modify
    task: Change the loop count in your program, then break it on purpose (remove
      the colon) and read what Python says.
    say: Python says there is a problem on line 3. I'm not going to guess. I read
      the line number, look at that line, and read the message slowly. It points
      at the colon after range. I put it back and run again. It worked, so the
      message told me where to look.
    notes: The first indentation or colon slip tends to happen in this lesson, so
      the strategy is used straight away. Do this once and move on; later
      lessons only nudge.
```
files.square.py:
# region: loop
from turtle import *

for i in range(4):
    forward(100)
    right(90)
# endregion

# region: modify
from turtle import *

for i in range(4):
    forward(100)
    right(90)

# Change the code so it draws a triangle.
# endregion

# region: make
from turtle import *

# Draw a staircase with a loop.
# endregion

# region: bug
from turtle import *

for i in range(4):
    forward(100)
right(90)
# endregion

# region: triangle
from turtle import *

for i in range(3):
    forward(100)
    right(120)
# endregion

# region: compare
# Without a loop
forward(100)
right(90)
forward(100)
right(90)
forward(100)
right(90)
forward(100)
right(90)

# With a loop
for i in range(4):
    forward(100)
    right(90)
# endregion

# region: sol-triangle
from turtle import *

for i in range(3):
    forward(100)
    right(120)
# endregion

# region: sol-stairs
from turtle import *

for i in range(5):
    left(90)
    forward(20)
    right(90)
    forward(20)
# endregion
